species.functional_description: Small passerine instantly recognisable by its orange breast, common in gardens and forests across France. Feeds mainly on earthworms, insects, and berries. Often follows gardeners and wild boar that turn over the soil.
Common passerine of forests and gardens. Nests in tree cavities, particularly in old beeches. Regulates insect populations in summer and switches to seeds in winter.
The most recognisable European woodpecker, known for its laughing call. Feeds mainly on ants, probing lawns and ant mounds. Excavates tree cavities that are later used by many other species.
species.keystone_description: Forest ecosystem engineer. Abandoned cavities shelter great tits, owls, bats, and kingfishers.

species.functional_description: Corvid renowned for its acorn-caching behaviour: a single bird buries several thousand acorns each autumn and forgets a portion, effectively planting oak trees. A key vector of forest regeneration.
species.keystone_description: Key seed disperser of oak forests. Transports acorns hundreds of metres, enabling colonisation of new areas and forest recovery after disturbance.

species.functional_description: Famous brood parasite that lays its eggs in the nests of other birds. One of the few species that consumes hairy caterpillars such as the pine processionary moth, playing a role in regulating some forest pests.

image.author: Andy  Morffew from Itchen Abbas, Hampshire, UK

species.functional_description: Small falcon famous for its characteristic hovering flight. Feeds mainly on voles and small mammals, providing natural rodent control over farmland.
species.keystone_description: Apex predator of open habitats. Controls vole and rodent populations, protecting crops and maintaining grassland balance.

species.functional_description: Powerful rooter that turns over the soil in search of acorns, beech mast, and underground fungi. Soil disturbance promotes plant diversity and creates opportunities for many species.
species.keystone_description: Forest soil engineer. Rooting creates germination microsites, disperses fungal spores, and maintains a mosaic of ground vegetation.

species.functional_description: Smallest native deer in France. Browses shoots, buds, and herbs, shaping the understorey vegetation. An important prey species for lynx and wolf where those predators are present.
Nocturnal insectivore of gardens, hedgerows, and woodland edges. Feeds on slugs, beetles, earthworms, and caterpillars — a valuable garden ally. Hibernates from October to March.
Powerful mustelid that digs extensive setts, aerating the soil. Its diet is roughly 80% earthworms. Abandoned setts are used by foxes, rabbits, and other species.
species.keystone_description: Architect of the forest subsoil. The sett networks it creates aerate the soil, improve water infiltration, and provide shelter for many species.

species.functional_description: Native squirrel of European forests. Caches seeds and nuts, a portion of which germinate and contribute to the dispersal of hazelnuts, acorns, and pine seeds. Depends on mature forest canopy.
Dominant tree of lowland French forests. Supports hundreds of insect species, nesting birds, and mammals. Acorns are a critical food resource for wild boar, deer, jays, and squirrels.
species.keystone_description: Foundation species of lowland forests. Structures the entire forest community by providing food, cavities, and habitat for hundreds of species.

species.functional_description: Climax dominant tree of many French hillside forests. Old beeches provide cavities for tits, owls, and bats. Beech mast feeds deer, wild boar, and small mammals in autumn.
species.keystone_description: Foundation species of the beech forest. Old beech cavities are a rare and essential resource for cavity-nesting species such as tits, treecreepers, and bats.

species.functional_description: Long cultivated and now naturalised across many French forests. Chestnuts provide an abundant autumn food resource for wild boar, deer, jays, and dormice.
Fast-growing shrub of forest edges and disturbed ground. Flowers attract pollinators; black berries feed blackbirds, thrushes, and small mammals in late summer.
Evergreen climber that flowers in autumn when few other plants are in bloom, offering late-season nectar to bees, hoverflies, and wasps. Winter berries feed pigeons and thrushes.
Larval host plant for several butterfly species including the European Peacock, Red Admiral, and Small Tortoiseshell. Indicates nitrogen-rich soil. A pioneer plant that boosts edge biodiversity.
Butterfly with distinctive eye-spot wings. Caterpillars feed exclusively on stinging nettles. Adults are important pollinators of wild and cultivated flowering plants.
Migratory butterfly that breeds on stinging nettles. Adults visit flowers and fermenting fruit. A regular garden visitor and generalist pollinator.
Long-lived butterfly that overwinters as an adult. One of the first to appear in spring. Caterpillars feed on buckthorn and alder buckthorn; adults pollinate from the first spring flowers.
France's largest butterfly, with yellow wings marked with black. Caterpillars feed on plants in the carrot family (Apiaceae), especially wild carrot. An important pollinator of flower-rich meadows.
Fundamental soil engineer that aerates, drains, and fertilises the ground by transforming organic matter. Primary food source for the European Robin, badger, hedgehog, woodcock, and many birds.
species.keystone_description: Essential soil engineer. Burrows improve soil structure, water infiltration, and nutrient availability for plants.

species.functional_description: Common wildflower of meadows and roadsides. Larval host plant of the Old World Swallowtail. The white umbel flowers attract a wide diversity of pollinators and hoverflies.

symbiosis.notes: The jay caches thousands of acorns each autumn to consume over winter. A portion is forgotten and germinates, making it the primary agent of oak forest regeneration and range expansion.
Earthworms are the robin's primary protein source, especially in autumn and winter. It regularly follows diggers — gardeners and wild boar — to pick up exposed worms.
Old World Swallowtail caterpillars feed on wild carrot leaves (and other Apiaceae). Adults pollinate the flowers when nectaring, providing cross-pollination for the plant.
Wild boar consume large quantities of acorns and chestnuts during the mast season (autumn). By rooting through the soil for buried fruit, they redistribute seeds and fungal spores.
The badger derives more than 80% of its food from earthworms. Its digging activity turns over the soil, creating favourable conditions for earthworm proliferation.
The great tit preferentially nests in old beech cavities. It benefits from the tree as a nesting site without causing any notable damage.
European Peacock caterpillars feed exclusively on stinging nettle. The relationship is critical for the butterfly; the plant benefits indirectly through pollination by the adults.
Stinging nettle is the Red Admiral's only larval host plant in France. Without nettles reproduction is impossible; adults in turn pollinate many wildflowers.
The squirrel caches acorns for later consumption. A significant percentage is never retrieved and germinates, contributing alongside the jay to oak dispersal and forest regeneration.
The green woodpecker excavates its nesting cavities in weakened or dead old beeches. Abandoned holes are subsequently colonised by tits, bats, and other cavity-nesting species.

relations.notes: The three principal forest trees of the French temperate zone, together forming the structure of deciduous woodland.
Four butterfly species representative of temperate French meadows and woodland edges.
Nettle-butterfly complex: stinging nettle is the essential larval host plant for both nymphalid species.
